title: Quantum communication and Bell nonlocality require infinite classical communication to simulate
authors: Carlos de Gois, Thyago S. R. Santos, Carlos Vieira
abstract: A quantum system of any fixed dimension can be prepared in a continuum of states, yet it cannot be used to transmit an unlimited amount of classical information. Similarly, the correlations observed between measurement outcomes on separate parts of a shared quantum system can be stronger than classical correlations, but they cannot transmit information. These fundamental limitations suggest that the statistics observed from quantum communication and quantum correlations may admit a simulation using a finite amount of classical communication. This expectation is confirmed in the smallest nontrivial quantum dimension, with two classical bits being necessary and sufficient to exactly simulate qubit communication and all correlations between qubits. Despite significant efforts during the previous decades, this remained the only solved case. Here we resolve both problems for every quantum dimension. The solution reveals an unexpected qualitative transition starting at dimension four: no finite amount of classical communication can exactly simulate ququart communication nor all quantum correlations of two entangled ququarts, even with unlimited shared randomness. One might have expected this transition, if it existed, to appear already for qutrits. Instead, we construct an explicit protocol that exactly simulates qutrit communication using $357$ classical bits, and consequently, all correlations of two entangled qutrits.
summary: This work determines the classical communication cost needed to simulate quantum communication and Bell nonlocality for arbitrary dimensions. It finds that while qubits and qutrits can be simulated with finite classical bits (though the cost for qutrits is high), any system with dimension four or higher requires an infinite amount of classical communication for exact simulation.
main_problem: The paper investigates the fundamental limits on simulating quantum communication and Bell nonlocality using only finite classical communication.
main_result: It establishes that for quantum dimensions $d_Q \geq 4$, no finite classical communication can simulate the quantum correlations, revealing a qualitative transition at $d_Q=4$.
method: The authors compare quantum probability distributions (derived from quantum measurements) against classical probability distributions achievable through finite classical encoding and shared randomness.
model_or_system: The study models quantum communication using states $ho$ of dimension $d_Q$ and local measurements $M$, and analyzes the simulation cost $C_{cl}(d_Q)$ required to match quantum statistics classically.
key_observables: The required classical communication dimension $d_C$, and the comparison between quantum and classical probability averages $p_Q$ vs $p_C$.
important_parameters: Quantum dimension $d_Q$ (e.g., 2 for qubits, 3 for qutrits, $\geq 4$ for ququarts), and the required classical bits $d_C$.
main_assumptions: The simulation model assumes a single round of classical communication (prepare-and-measure model).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the setup for classical simulation (prepare-and-measure model) and show the comparison of quantum vs. classical averages, particularly highlighting the divergence for ququarts.
paper_structure: The paper first addresses the general simulation problem, solving it for qubits ($d_Q=2$) and constructing an explicit, large protocol for qutrits ($d_Q=3$). It then proves that for $d_Q \geq 4$, the simulation cost is infinite, marking a sharp transition.
why_interesting: The finding that quantum correlations require infinite classical resources above a certain dimension is a fundamental statement about the non-classical nature of quantum information, relevant to understanding the resource theory of quantum communication.

(a) In the communication setting, a quantum state ρ of dimension dQ is communicated to a measurement device. Given a measurement M, an outcome b is produced with probability pQ(b | ρ, M). In a classical simulation, the quantum system is encoded in a message c of finite dimension using unlimited shared randomness, and decoded producing b with probability pC(b | ρ, M). A classical simulation exists if there is an encoder and decoder functions realizing pC(b | ρ, M) = pQ(b | ρ, M) for all possible inputs ρ and M.
